title: Justice (ST II-II.58)

segments.voice: Yesterday, prudence: right reason applied to action, ending not in thinking but in doing. Your line was think, then act. Which decision did you follow through on? Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

The neighbor's ladder has been leaning in the garage since spring. It was borrowed for one afternoon. Nobody's angry. Nobody's even asked for it back. But every time the garage door goes up, there it is, quietly saying something. Or a coworker came up with the idea that saved the project, and in the big meeting it somehow came out sounding like yours. Nobody lied, exactly. But something is owed and hasn't been paid. Yesterday, prudence held the reins. Today Thomas names the virtue that faces outward, toward everyone else. Justice.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER, STILL HERE.` → `AN IDEA THAT WASN'T YOURS.` → `SOMETHING IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Thomas takes his definition from the old Roman lawyers and makes it his own. Justice, he says, is a habit by which a person, with a constant and lasting will, gives to each one what is their due. Look at the pieces. To each one: not to the people you like, or the ones who can pay you back. Each. Their due: what belongs to them, what they have a right to. Credit for their work. The truth. Wages on time. A fair hearing. Their ladder. And then the word that's easiest to skip: steadily. Thomas says justice lives in a constant will. One fair act on a good day isn't yet the virtue. Justice is being the kind of person who returns what's owed as a matter of course, the habit from two days ago, aimed outward. Here's what makes justice different from the other virtues, in Thomas's account. The other moral virtues, he says, set a person right inside: calm when angry, brave when afraid. Justice is always about someone else. It's the virtue of the relationship. So you can't do justice alone in a room. It needs a neighbor. And Thomas widens the circle as far as it goes. Even God is owed something: honor, worship, thanks. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says it in one breath: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God, the things that are God's." Justice, for Thomas, isn't first a courtroom or a protest sign, though it reaches both. It starts with the ladder in the garage.
screen: `TO EACH ONE, THEIR DUE.` · `A CONSTANT AND LASTING WILL.` · `ALWAYS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE.` · `EVEN GOD IS OWED SOMETHING.` · then, large: `RENDER TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone their due. Settle, and breathe. Let the faces of the people around you come to mind, one at a time. Family. Coworkers. A neighbor. Someone who serves you coffee. For each, ask quietly: is there something I owe here that I haven't given? Thanks. Credit. A returned call. Money. An apology. A fair hearing for someone you've written off. Don't make a list of everything. Let one rise to the top, the clearest one. Decide what giving it would look like today. If you pray, you can name that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Justice. For Thomas, a steady will to give each person what is their due, a virtue that always faces someone else. Today's word.
Your line: each their due. Today, pay one small debt that nobody is chasing you for: the credit, the thanks, or the ladder. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts justice among the four cardinal virtues, describing it as the constant will to give God and neighbor their due, and Catholic social teaching applies it to wages, work and the common good.

fork.reveal: for Thomas, justice gives each their due whether or not anyone is chasing it. credit for their work belongs to them.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: justice, giving each their due.

trapdoor: what you thought: justice means punishment, or a courtroom.
what it means: a steady will to give each person, and God, what is their due.
what a scholar hears: Thomas adopts the Roman lawyers' definition, a constant and perpetual will to render to each his right, and places it in the will.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: the definition of justice taken from the Roman jurists, 'a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will' (II-II.58.1); justice is always toward another (II-II.58.2); justice in the will (II-II.58.4); religion, rendering God due worship, as a virtue annexed to justice (II-II.81).
'Most virtues set a person right inside' is the script's summary of II-II.58.2 (other moral virtues concern the passions, justice concerns another); confirm the wording doesn't overstate.
The large screen line shortens Matthew 22:21 for display; the voice quotes it in full.
Editor: the teach pointed to 'steadily' in today's hook, but the spoken hook never says it; the reference was removed.
